references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Under the Food Act 2001 all food businesses must notify the appropriate enforcement agency, usually the local council, before opening, using the council's Food Business Notification form (or SA Health's form where the council has none or the business is outside a council area). There is no fee for notification. Penalties for not notifying are up to $120,000 for a body corporate and $25,000 for an individual (expiation $1,500 and $300). Businesses captured by Standard 3.2.2A, such as cafes, restaurants, supermarkets, mobile food vans and takeaways, must appoint a certified food safety supervisor, and food handlers of high-risk unpackaged food must be trained. Mobile food businesses notify the council where the vehicle is normally garaged; caterers where most food or equipment is stored.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Any person or business operating as a building work contractor must be licensed, including sub-contractors. All building work must be supervised by a registered building work supervisor. Licences cover general or specified building work; specified work needs at least $10,000 net assets, or a restricted subcontractor licence. Builders in major residential construction attach a certificate of eligibility for building indemnity insurance. Apply online, print, sign, scan and upload; National Police Certificate no more than 12 months old. rule_sets.title: South Australia: business licences, insurance and tax
rule_sets.description: Registrations, licences, insurance and tax most SA businesses check: food business notification, food safety supervisors, liquor licences, outdoor dining, ReturnToWorkSA registration and payroll tax.
limitations: Built from SA Health, Consumer and Business Services, ReturnToWorkSA and RevenueSA web pages, not from the Acts themselves.
Does not decide which liquor licence you need. We use the restaurant and catering licence as the example; bars, small venues and bottle shops use other licence classes.
Outdoor dining rules are set by each council; we show them as something to check.
Does not check planning consent (development approval) for the use of your premises or a fit-out.
Not legal or tax advice. Confirm with the regulator or a qualified professional before you rely on it.

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Notify your local council before you open
outcomes.detail: Under the Food Act 2001 (SA) every food business must notify the enforcement agency before it opens. That is usually your local council's environmental health team. Lodge the council's food business notification form. There is no fee to notify, but councils may charge for inspections. Food vans notify the council where the van is normally garaged, and caterers notify the council where most food or equipment is stored. Trading without notifying can bring a fine of up to $25,000 for an individual or $120,000 for a company.

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.detail: SA payroll tax applies when your total Australian taxable wages (including grouped businesses) are more than $1.5 million a year, or $125,000 a month, and you pay wages in SA. rule_sets.title: South Australia: building, plumbing, gas fitting and electrical licences
rule_sets.description: Building work contractor licences and supervisor registration, building indemnity insurance, and plumbing, gas fitting and electrical licences from Consumer and Business Services.
limitations: Built from sa.gov.au Consumer and Business Services pages and a PlanSA advisory notice, not from the Building Work Contractors Act 1995 or the Plumbers, Gas Fitters and Electricians Act 1995 directly.
In SA any building work contractor needs a licence; the CBS page sets no minimum dollar value, so we treat small building jobs as needing one too.
Our question about building work uses a $3,300 line set for Queensland. SA building indemnity insurance starts at $20,000, so it is shown as likely, not certain.
Gas fitting has no separate answer in our questions; it is shown under plumbing and 'other trade'.
Security, second-hand goods and other occupational licences are not covered.
Not legal advice. Confirm with CBS Licensing (131 882, option 4) before you rely on it.

outcomes.title: You need a building work contractor's licence

All building work must be supervised by a registered building work supervisor: sole traders usually apply for the licence and supervisor registration together, and companies nominate a supervisor. Apply online, then print, sign, scan and upload the form with a police certificate no more than 12 months old. An individual's general building work licence with supervisor registration costs $1,139; a company's general building work licence costs $1,575.

rule_sets.title: South Australia: registering and selling imported vehicles
rule_sets.description: Inspecting and registering an imported vehicle in SA (Department for Infrastructure and Transport and Service SA), stamp duty, and the CBS second-hand vehicle dealer licence for resale.

rules.title: Registering the vehicle in SA
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Get the vehicle inspected, then register it at Service SA
outcomes.detail: An imported vehicle must pass an identity inspection before any modifications, at the Department for Infrastructure and Transport's inspection station at 7 Naweena Road, Regency Park (no booking needed; phone 8400 8777). You need an unregistered vehicle permit or trade plates to drive it there. Then get a roadworthy inspection ($344, booked) if required, and a compliance plate exemption for personal imports. Take your import approval or Register of Approved Vehicles entry, the inspection certificates and the SA application for registration and compulsory third party insurance (MR1) to a Service SA centre. You pay registration and CTP (about $705 a year for a 4-cylinder car in Adelaide), the $75 identity inspection fee, number plates and stamp duty on the market value unless duty was already paid in another Australian state.

rules.title: Selling imported vehicles in SA
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: You need a second-hand vehicle dealer's licence to sell imported vehicles
outcomes.detail: In SA you must hold a second-hand vehicle dealer's licence from Consumer and Business Services if you buy, sell or offer for sale 4 or more vehicles in 12 months. Used imports count as second-hand vehicles. Apply online, then print, sign, scan and upload the form with a National Police Certificate no more than 12 months old. An individual licence for cars and motorcycles costs $952 plus a $200 compensation fund contribution ($1,243 plus $200 for a company). You can only trade from the premises registered on your licence, and companies must nominate a licensed manager.

outcomes.title: Register the boat through Service SA
outcomes.detail: Recreational motorboats in SA must be registered with the Department for Infrastructure and Transport. Fill in the SA application for initial boat registration (MR168), measure the hull from bow to transom, and lodge it at a Service SA centre (or post it to GPO Box 1533, Adelaide SA 5001) with proof of ownership and ID. A Hull Identification Number check may be needed. Twelve-month fees in 2026-27 range from $59 (under 3.1 m) to $174 (3.5 to 5 m) and $484 for a jet ski; a 50% discount applies until 1 December 2026.

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: You need an SA boat operator's licence
outcomes.detail: You must hold a current boat operator's licence to operate any recreational vessel fitted with an engine in SA, whatever its size. Without one you can only drive a motorboat if you're at least 12, supervised by a licence holder and stay at or under 10 knots. Pass the boat operator's licence theory test ($56), then apply in person at a Service SA centre with original ID (licence $53). Children aged 12 to 15 can get a special permit instead.
